start.title: Site Crashes 2 Minutes Before Sales Open
start.bestWhy: Activate traffic filtering to stop the flood first, then delay the sale opening transparently. That loses fewer fans than guessing your way through fixes.
start.text: You run the ticket sales website for a university band. Sales open at 10:00 AM, but at 9:58 AM traffic (the number of requests hitting the site) spikes 50x, coming from thousands of machines worldwide. The site crashes. 1,000 genuine fans waiting to buy can't get in. What do you do first?
start.source: Cloudflare Learning Center: What is a DDoS attack?; CISA: Understanding and Responding to DDoS Attacks

choices.label: Enable the hosting provider's DDoS protection service, then announce a postponement of the sale opening.
choices.out: You delay the sale by about 6 hours. Some fans are frustrated, but fake traffic gets filtered out, the site recovers, and you have time to read the logs and understand what happened.
u: Sale delayed 6 hours — some fans don't wait.
choices.lesson: A DDoS attack floods a site with fake requests until it can't respond. The fix is filtering out the fake traffic before it reaches the site, then figuring out who did it and why.

choices.label: Keep restarting the server until the site comes back up.
choices.out: The site comes back for a few seconds then crashes again. Fans keep refreshing all day, and you still have no idea where the traffic is coming from.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Restarting treats the symptom, not the cause. As long as fake traffic keeps hitting the site, it will keep crashing.

choices.label: Block the top 10 IPs sending the most requests — assuming it's one person doing this.
choices.out: Traffic drops only slightly, because requests are coming from thousands of machines. And some of the blocked IPs belong to student dormitories where real fans are.
u: Some real fans accidentally blocked.
choices.lesson: Base your hypothesis on evidence. A DDoS comes from large numbers of controlled machines (a botnet). Blocking individual IPs doesn't work and may block real users.

choices.label: Cancel this sale round, move the site to the biggest server you can find, and rewrite the ticketing system from scratch.
choices.out: You spend two weeks building a new system. Server costs jump significantly, many fans lose interest while waiting — but the new system can handle far more load.
u: Sale cancelled — many fans lost.
choices.lesson: A bigger server can handle more load, but a large-scale DDoS can always send more traffic than any single server can absorb. Filtering fake traffic is the more cost-effective solution.

investigate.title: Who Crashed the Site and Why?
investigate.bestWhy: There are two simultaneous root causes — both must be closed: filter fake traffic and enforce purchase limits server-side.
investigate.text: From the logs you find that the crash was just a cover. While real fans were locked out, bots (automated programs) run by ticket scalpers fired purchase commands directly at the system and grabbed 40% of all tickets, which are now being resold on social media at 5x the original price. There are two root causes: (1) there was no traffic filtering in place, and (2) the system has no per-person ticket limit and no way to tell whether a buyer is human or a bot. How do you fix this?
investigate.source: OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications (Scalping); CISA: Understanding and Responding to DDoS Attacks

choices.label: Enable permanent traffic filtering, set up a queue, limit tickets to 4 per person, and verify buyers are human at the Server — then cancel the bot orders before reopening sales.
choices.out: You spend one day setting everything up, cancel the bot orders and return the tickets to the pool, then try firing bot-style purchase commands yourself — the system rejects all of them.
u: Sale delayed another half day.
choices.lesson: Protect at both layers: filter fake traffic so the site doesn't crash, and enforce purchase rules at the Server — because bots don't use your webpage the way humans do.

choices.label: Enable traffic filtering first — deal with the ticket-buying bots later.
choices.out: The site no longer crashes. You reopen sales quickly, but there's still no per-person ticket limit and no bot detection.
u: Brief sale delay.
choices.lesson: A half-fix creates a false sense of completion — but the real goal of the attack (getting tickets) is still achievable.

choices.label: Limit tickets to 4 per person, then push the code change to the live site immediately without testing — fans are waiting.
choices.out: The ticket limit works. You reopen sales quickly, but the untested code hasn't been properly reviewed, and traffic filtering still isn't enabled.
u: Brief sale delay.
choices.lesson: Being in a rush shouldn't be a reason to skip testing. Try the fix on a staging copy first, then push it live.

partialClient.title: Bots Sweep the Second Round
partialClient.bestWhy: Purchase rules must be enforced at the Server. Hiding or checking things on the webpage — bots can always bypass that.
partialClient.text: Five days later, the second round of sales opens. The site doesn't crash this time — but bots sweep 60% of all tickets within the first minute, which are immediately listed on social media at 5x the price. Genuine fans are furious and start tagging the band.

u: Bots sweep tickets — real fans can't buy.

partialClient.source: OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications (Scalping); OWASP Top 10: Insecure Design

choices.label: Enforce per-person ticket limits and bot detection at the Server, set up a queue, and cancel orders that came from bots.
choices.out: You cancel the suspicious orders, re-release those tickets through the queue, and this time all bot attempts are rejected. Real fans get their tickets.
u: Sales paused to apply the fix.
choices.lesson: Important rules (like tickets per person) must be enforced at the Server — because bots don't use your webpage. They send purchase requests directly to the system.

choices.label: Hide the buy button until sales open, and add code on the webpage to allow only one click at a time.
choices.out: The webpage looks cleaner, but bots don't click buttons on a screen. They send purchase commands directly to the system and bypass these checks within the hour.
u: Bots bypass the client-side check successfully.
choices.lesson: Client-side checks (webpage checks) improve the user experience but are not security — attackers have full control over their own client.

partialRules.title: Confirmation Emails Sent to the Wrong People
partialRules.bestWhy: Fix everything completely, check what data was exposed and to whom, and notify all affected people.
partialRules.text: Five days later, the second round of sales opens. The site gets flooded again because traffic filtering still isn't in place, and in the chaos, the untested code change causes a bug: confirmation emails are sent to the wrong people. 2,100 buyers each see another person's name, phone number, and seat number.

u: Fans who saw leaked data — some request refunds.

choices.label: Fix the code and enable traffic filtering, check which emails went to whom, then notify all 2,100 affected buyers directly with an apology.
choices.out: You email all 2,100 people explaining what data was exposed and what to watch out for. Some are angry, but many thank you for being upfront.
u: Some fans request refunds after being notified.
choices.lesson: Notifying affected people honestly hurts in the short term, but it lets them protect themselves. (International data protection law such as the EU's GDPR requires notifying the supervisory authority within 72 hours and notifying affected individuals when the risk is high.)

choices.label: Fix the code quietly and don't announce it — you think people probably didn't notice.
choices.out: The system returns to normal, but people who received someone else's data start asking on social media why they got a stranger's email.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Staying silent doesn't make the problem go away — it just hides the damage until it surfaces, and when it does, the trust loss will be far worse.

choices.label: Suspend sales and bring in an external expert to audit the whole system before making any announcement.
choices.out: The expert finds two more bugs and confirms exactly what data was exposed. You announce with a clear remediation plan, but sales have to stay suspended for a long time at significant cost.
u: Extended suspension — some fans don't wait.
choices.lesson: External experts are worth it when you're unsure of the damage scope — but you need to weigh the cost against the time your service has to stay down.

repeat.title: Crashed Again
repeat.bestWhy: Being hit again means the root cause is still there. Stop, fix everything properly, and communicate honestly.
repeat.text: A new sale round opens. The site crashes from the first minute and bots sweep nearly all the tickets. Real fans get nothing, and the tickets show up on social media at many times the original price. What do you do?
repeat.source: CISA: Understanding and Responding to DDoS Attacks; OWASP Automated Threats to Web Applications

choices.label: Suspend sales, enable traffic filtering, enforce ticket limits and bot detection at the Server, cancel bot orders, then communicate openly about what happened.
choices.out: You fix both root causes completely, cancel the bot tickets, and make an honest announcement. Fans are upset, but most see that you're taking responsibility.
u: Sales suspended — some fans lost from the news.
choices.lesson: Being attacked again means the first round didn't fix the root cause. Stop, review the evidence, fix everything completely, and communicate straightforwardly.

choices.label: Fix the system completely, but don't tell anyone that the previous tickets ended up with bots.
choices.out: The system is genuinely more secure — but fans who bought tickets from scalpers at inflated prices don't know what happened.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Concealing an incident doesn't protect users — it only delays the day the truth comes out.

choices.label: Give out discount codes and add more show dates to win fans back — fix the system later.
choices.out: Orders spike immediately, but bots get the discount codes too, and they sweep the new round alongside real fans.
u: Discount codes bring some fans back.
choices.lesson: Polishing your image without fixing the system just delays the problem — and it comes back harder.

rewrite.title: New System, New Holes
rewrite.tag: New Vulnerabilities from a Rushed Build
rewrite.bestWhy: Close the admin panel vulnerabilities before going live — multiple layers (login rate limiting + a second factor) are safer than waiting for something to go wrong.
rewrite.text: Two weeks later the new ticketing system launches. It has traffic filtering, a queue system, and per-person ticket limits. Some fans come back following the news. But in the rush, you forgot to change the admin panel's default password and didn't limit failed login attempts. A bot is now trying to guess the admin password about 3,000 times per hour.

u: Some fans return following the relaunch news.

rewrite.source: CISA Secure by Design (no default passwords); NIST SP 800-63B (limit login attempts)

choices.label: Change the default password, enable two-factor authentication (2-step) for the admin account, and limit failed login attempts.
choices.out: The bot keeps trying but gets blocked after just a few failed attempts — and even if it guesses the password right, it still can't get in without the code from your phone.
u: Fans feel confident as the system stays stable.
choices.lesson: Defence in depth: rate limiting + a second factor means a weak or leaked password is no longer a single point of failure.

choices.label: Only change the default password to a longer one.
choices.out: A longer password helps a lot, but the bot can still try an unlimited number of times — and there's still no second factor if the password is phished.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: A strong password is a good first layer — but it shouldn't be the only layer.

choices.label: Don't do it right now — need to open the new sale round first.
choices.out: First-day sales are great — but that night the bot successfully guesses the admin password.
u: New sale round pays off.
choices.lesson: A risk that hasn't materialized yet is not a risk that doesn't exist. A bot actively guessing passwords is clear evidence the system is already being targeted.

wave2.title: Fake Email from the Payment Processor
wave2.bestWhy: Check through a channel you navigate yourself — not a link in the email — and add a second factor to important accounts.
wave2.text: About a week passes. The previous holes are closed, but the attacker changes tactics. You receive an email claiming to be from the payment company the website uses, saying: "Suspicious activity detected — your payment account will be suspended in 24 hours if you don't verify your identity." The logo and wording look completely genuine.
wave2.source: CISA Secure Our World: Recognize and Report Phishing; Verizon DBIR

choices.label: Don't click the link. Open the payment company's website by typing the address yourself, check for any real alerts, and enable 2-step for all admin accounts.
choices.out: There are no alerts on the real account. You recognize it as phishing, enable 2-step for all admin accounts, and warn the team not to click links in emails like this.
u: System stable — fans return to buy.
choices.lesson: An urgent email + a threat to suspend your account + a link is the classic phishing signal. Always verify through a channel you navigate yourself.

choices.label: Click the link — if it looks real, enter your password, because you're afraid of not being able to receive payments.
choices.out: The page is a fake that captures your password. A few hours later someone logs into the ticket site's admin panel using those credentials.
u: No visible effect yet.
choices.lesson: Urgency is a phishing tool. Reusing the same password in multiple places means one compromise takes down everything.

choices.label: Delete the email and do nothing more.
choices.out: You dodge this one — but you haven't checked your accounts or added a second factor. If a more convincing email comes next, there's nothing to fall back on.
u: No additional incidents.
choices.lesson: Not being fooled this time doesn't mean you're safe. Adding a second factor (2-step) means a leaked password won't bring down the whole system.

takeover.title: Admin Account Hijacked
takeover.bestWhy: You need to cut the attacker off from every access point — not just change the password. Then audit what they changed.
takeover.text: The attacker is inside the ticket site's admin panel using a legitimate admin account. They changed the payment receiving account to their own, created 200 free VIP tickets for themselves, and viewed buyer data — all without exploiting a single line of code.

u: Payment account altered — many fans lost.

takeover.source: NIST SP 800-61 (incident response); OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet

choices.label: Log out every active session, change passwords on all accounts, enable 2-step, audit the logs for what was changed, cancel the fake tickets, restore the payment account, and notify buyers.
choices.out: You go through every change one by one, cancel all fake tickets, restore the original payment account, close every access point, and notify buyers directly.
u: Sales paused for remediation — some fans request refunds after being notified.
choices.lesson: When an account is hijacked, you must cut the attacker off from every access point — active sessions, tokens, and keys — not just change the password. Then audit everything they touched.

choices.label: Change the password only, then resume sales.
choices.out: The attacker is still logged in on their device. They come back the next night and change the payment account again.
u: Brief pause to change the password.
Attacker returns via the still-active session.
choices.lesson: Changing the password alone isn't enough. If the attacker still has an active session, they can keep coming back. You must log them out of every device.

choices.label: Hire an external security team to audit the entire backend, then follow their recommendations.
choices.out: The team discovers the attacker created a hidden admin account. They remove it, set up 2-step, and buyers are notified. Costly, but thorough.
u: Extended suspension and audit fees — some fans don't wait.
choices.lesson: Attackers often leave a "backdoor" behind. Expert eyes can find things you'd miss — but it comes at a cost in time and money.

news.title: The Story Breaks on Social Media
news.bestWhy: If you missed the disclosure window, admit it and act as soon as you realize. The longer you stay silent, the more trust you lose.
news.text: A fan posts a screenshot of a confirmation email containing someone else's name and phone number, and describes how a ticket bought from a scalper wouldn't scan at the gate. The post is shared thousands of times overnight, and people start asking whether the organizer knew about this.

u: News breaks that the organizer covered up the incident.

news.source: EU GDPR Article 34 (notification of affected individuals)

choices.label: Issue a public statement acknowledging what happened, what was fixed, and telling fans what they should do next.
choices.out: You admit you knew earlier and didn't notify anyone. The criticism is heavy — but the clear information keeps some fans on your side.
u: Some fans stop following after learning they were kept in the dark.
choices.lesson: If you missed the disclosure, fix it the moment you realize. Late transparency is still better than none.

choices.label: Say the screenshot is fake and has nothing to do with the website.
choices.out: Multiple users post more screenshots from the same system. The denial gets shared as a textbook example of an irresponsible organizer.
u: Caught denying verifiable facts.
choices.lesson: Denying verifiable facts turns a data incident into a full-blown credibility crisis.

choices.label: Suspend sales for three days to investigate before issuing any statement.
choices.out: You confirm the full scope of the damage before speaking — but during those three silent days, the rumours travel further than the facts.
u: Three days of silence — rumours spread.
choices.lesson: Verifying before speaking is good — but if you go silent too long, rumours will tell the story for you.

wave2_blocked.title: Phishing That Failed
wave2_blocked.text: The following week, a fake email impersonating the payment company reaches your team. One admin already entered their password on the fake page — but the attacker can't get into the account, because every admin account has 2-step enabled. You receive an alert about a login attempt from an unknown device.

u: Fans see the system running smoothly — no incidents.

wave2_blocked.source: Microsoft Security: MFA blocks nearly all automated account takeovers

choices.label: View summary
choices.out: You change that admin's password and remind the team to stay alert. No damage is done.
u: No damage.
choices.lesson: A second factor means one person's mistake doesn't become a disaster for the whole system.

root.title: An Organizer Fans Can Trust
root.desc: You filtered fake traffic, stopped the bots, layered your defences, and genuine fans got most of their tickets.

rebuilder.title: The Architect Who Started Over
rebuilder.desc: You took the most expensive path — a full rebuild — and still caught the new vulnerabilities that came with the rush. The system is secure, but the fanbase is not the same.

honest.title: Honest but Bruised
honest.desc: This event took a serious hit, but you told fans the truth. The trust that remains is the foundation for the next event.

survivor.title: A Survivor Who Learned
survivor.desc: The ticket site is still running and the critical holes are closed — even if there were costs along the way.

nomfa.title: Strong on Fixes, Forgot the Second Layer
nomfa.desc: Traffic and bots are handled, but admin accounts still rely on a password alone. The remaining risk is a human one.

cover.title: Covered It Up and Lost the Trust
cover.desc: The system may have been fixed — but not telling fans only delayed the damage, and when it hit, it hit harder.

scarred.title: Deep Wounds, Still Standing
scarred.desc: The event's revenue and data took serious damage. It can still go ahead, but rebuilding fan trust will take a long time.

bleeding.title: Bleeding Out
bleeding.desc: You attracted fans with promotions instead of fixing the system. Bots and attackers exploit the same holes every round. The event is slowly falling apart with no end to the incident in sight.

collapse.title: The Event Had to Be Cancelled
collapse.desc: The fanbase dropped too low to continue. Look back and see which decision caused the biggest drop.

AXES.dL: You tend to keep the ticket site running first, even when risk remains.
AXES.dR: You're willing to lose users in the short term to secure the system first.
AXES.dM: You strike a reasonable balance between security and keeping the ticket site running.

AXES.dL: You prefer to verify before acting. The upside is precision; the downside is speed.
AXES.dR: You decide quickly. The upside is stopping incidents fast; the downside is missing things.
AXES.dM: You adjust your pace well to the demands of each situation.

AXES.dL: You tend to prioritize image — which often erodes user trust later.
AXES.dR: You tell users the truth, even when it stings in the short term.
AXES.dM: You haven't faced many situations that forced a clear communication choice yet.

AXES.dL: You tend to choose the fast fix, which sometimes leaves the root cause untouched.
AXES.dR: You think about root causes and long-term consequences.
AXES.dM: You mix quick patches with root-cause fixes.
